# Export & extend {#sec-export-and-extend}



::: {.callout-note title="What you'll be able to do"}
Save a publication-ready figure to PDF, generate a parameterised PDF report of your own run, and
point yourself toward the model's natural extensions.
:::

## Getting things out as PDF

There are two senses of "PDF output", and the workshop gives you both.

**The whole workshop as a PDF.** Use the **Download PDF** link in the sidebar — Quarto renders this
entire site to a single document from the same source you have been reading.

**A figure as a vector PDF.** For your own results, `ggsave()` writes a clean, scalable PDF you can
drop straight into a manuscript. Build the figure once, then save it:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
out <- MPM(h2 = 0.2, Vp = 1, Beta = 0.15,
           Fe = species$F[3], SA = species$SA[3], SJ = species$SJ[3],
           S0 = species$SJ[3], Y = species$gamma[3], selectedrate = "SJ")

p <- out$pheno_distribution |>
  filter(year %in% seq(1, 101, by = 25)) |>
  ggplot(aes(phenotypic_midvalue, density, colour = factor(year))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "mako", direction = -1, name = "Year") +
  labs(x = "Phenotype value", y = "Density",
       title = "Passerine under juvenile-survival selection")
p
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-export-and-extend_files/figure-html/build-summary-fig-1.png){width=1400}
:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggsave("my_figure.pdf", p, width = 7, height = 4.2, device = cairo_pdf)
```
:::


**A full parameterised report.** The repository ships a template at `templates/report.qmd`. Render it
to PDF for any species and selection scenario without editing the file — just pass parameters:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
quarto::quarto_render(
  "templates/report.qmd",
  execute_params = list(species_id = 5, rate = "SA", beta = 0.3, h2 = 0.2)
)
```
:::


This is the reproducible way to hand a collaborator a tidy PDF for a specific run: the parameters are
recorded in the document itself.

## Extending the model

The two-stage life cycle with one trait is a teaching scaffold. The same framework reaches further —
here is where to look next, all grounded in the original paper [@vandewalle2025].

**Phenotypic plasticity.** In the base model an individual keeps its phenotype for life (the
within-life phenotype-transition matrices $\mathbf{P}_{ij}$ are identities). Make them *non-identity*
and a trait can change with age or with the environment — that is plasticity, expressed in exactly the
same matrix language as evolution.

**Two-sex inheritance.** The model tracks male *and* female breeding values, so paternal
contributions enter the inheritance step explicitly.

**Evolving genetic variance.** The base model holds $V_A$, $V_P$ and $h^2$ at birth constant. The
authors note that letting $V_A$ vary is computationally cheap to add, though it requires committing to
assumptions about genetic architecture.

**Richer life cycles.** Nothing restricts the demography to two stages. The vec-permutation
construction scales to any stage-structured life cycle — including the kinds of long-lived marine and
terrestrial vertebrates these methods were built for.

## Capstone — your turn

::: {.callout-important title="A question to take home"}
Pick a species you actually study (or the closest of our five). Decide which vital rate selection most
plausibly acts on, and which **definition** of adaptation rate answers your real question — per year
for a management horizon, per generation for a genetic one. Run it, plot the trait distribution
through time, and export a one-figure PDF. You now have a reproducible eco-evolutionary projection for
your system — and a clear-eyed sense of what its adaptation rate does and does not mean.
:::

## Where the code lives

- **Package** (install from here): the `evodemohypermpm` repository on the CNRS Koda forge.
- **Full code** (MATLAB + R + the individual-based model): `fledge-whoi/Eco-EvoHyperstateModel` on GitHub.
- **Reproduction archive** for the paper's figures: the project's Zenodo deposit.
- **The paper**: Van de Walle, Garnier, Bonnet & Jenouvrier (2025), *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*
  [@vandewalle2025] — the citation for any work using the model.

Thank you for working through it. Go model an adaptation rate, and report the number rather than
guessing it.
